cap.1.1-b1.01: Oops! Soft landing... mostly. Hi! I'm VIMO. I'm an astronaut, and I look after some very special friends. They live far, far away.
cap.1.1-b2.01: Wait, VIMO, who lives up there?
cap.1.1-b2.02: Machines! Cameras, landers, rovers, even a helicopter. NASA sent them to the Moon and Mars to explore. When their work was done, they stayed there.
cap.1.1-b3.01: Some people call them space junk. I don't. Each one has a story: where it went, what it did, and what it taught us. Tonight, you and I will visit them. Ready?
cap.1.2-b4.01: See that thin blue line? That's our air. Above it is space: no air to breathe, no sound, and it's freezing in the shade and boiling in the sunlight.
cap.1.2-b5.01: Why can't we just fly up there?
cap.1.2-b5.02: Earth pulls everything down. That's gravity. To escape it, a rocket must go about 40,000 kilometres per hour. That's 30 times faster than a jet plane!
cap.1.2-b6.01: If Earth were a basketball, the Moon would be a tennis ball about seven metres away. In real life that's about 384,000 kilometres. In a car, it would take you more than 5 months, with no stops!
cap.1.3-b7.01: Hold on tight! Three... two... one... lift-off! Our first stop is 1964, when NASA was still learning how to even reach the Moon.
cap.1.3-b8.01: Fun fact: in space there's no up or down, so I can read upside down. Look, the year counter! We're going back in time to 1964. That's before your grandparents were teenagers, maybe!
cap.2.1-b1.01: Meet Ranger 7! In 1964, nobody had ever seen the Moon up close. So NASA sent a camera... and let it crash.
cap.2.1-b2.01: Click! Click! Click! I took pictures all the way down. I didn't need to land. I just needed to look!
cap.2.1-b2.02: In its last 17 minutes, Ranger 7 sent more than 4,000 photos. They were the closest pictures of the Moon anyone had ever seen.
cap.2.1-b2.try: See? The closer you get, the more you can see.
cap.2.1-b3.01: Scientists even gave the place a new name: the Sea that has Become Known. Ranger 7 is still there, in pieces, right where it learned the Moon's first secrets. Thank you, Ranger 7!
cap.2.2-b4.01: Some scientists worried the Moon was covered in deep dust. Like soft flour. Would a spacecraft sink? Would an astronaut sink? Someone had to test it.
cap.2.2-b5.01: Touchdown! And look: my feet are on top of the dust, not under it. The ground is strong!
cap.2.2-b5.02: Surveyor 1 was America's first soft landing on the Moon. It sent more than 11,000 photos. Now NASA knew: people could land here too.
cap.2.2-b5.try: So that's how rockets slow you down.
cap.2.2-b6.01: Thank you, Surveyor 1. You took the Moon's first safe step, so astronauts could take the next one.
cap.2.3-b7.01: This is Surveyor 3. It landed in 1967, dug the Moon's soil with a little scoop, and sent photos home. Then it went quiet. Alone. For two and a half years.
cap.2.3-b8.01: Then, in November 1969, Apollo 12 landed close by. Two astronauts walked over to say hello!
cap.2.3-b8.02: Visitors! I knew someone would come back.
cap.2.3-b9.01: Why did they take its camera?
cap.2.3-b9.02: To see what two and a half years on the Moon does to a machine. Its parts came home for scientists to study. Surveyor 3 helped us twice!
cap.2.3-b9b.01: I landed so precisely that the astronauts could walk to an old robot parked nearby.
cap.2.3-b9b.02: Apollo 12 also left a science station. When its top part was crashed into the Moon later, the Moon 'rang' like a bell for nearly an hour!
cap.2.3-b9b.try: So that's how we listen to the inside of the Moon.
cap.2.4-b10.01: This is it. July 1969. The first time people walked on another world. And this is their ship, the Eagle.
cap.2.4-b11.01: Hey, half of it stayed behind!
cap.2.4-b11.02: That's the plan! The bottom half was the launch pad. The astronauts flew home in the top half. The bottom half is still standing there today.
cap.2.4-b12.01: My plaque says: 'We came in peace for all mankind.' I've been holding that message for more than 55 years.
cap.2.4-b12.02: Footprints, tools and the Eagle's bottom half are all still there. There's no wind on the Moon, so footprints can last a very long time.
cap.2.5-b13.01: Most of the machines we visit tonight are finished. But this little box is still working. Right now. Watch!
cap.2.5-b14.01: Ping! Ping! Every beam you send, I send back. Same way, every time!
cap.2.5-b14.02: Scientists measure how long the light takes. That's how we know the Moon is moving away from Earth, about 3.8 centimetres every year. That's how fast your fingernails grow!
cap.2.5-b14.try: So that's how light measures the distance to the Moon.
cap.2.6-b15.01: Boing... boing... And in 1971, astronauts brought a car! It came folded up, like a paper toy.
cap.2.6-b16.01: Battery power, wire-mesh wheels and no road at all. I drove the astronauts about 28 kilometres. Not bad for a car that fits in a suitcase... a big suitcase.
cap.2.6-b16.02: Why mesh wheels and not rubber tyres?
cap.2.6-b16.03: No air means no air-filled tyres. So its wheels were woven from thin steel wire, like a basket!
cap.2.6-b17.01: The rover is still parked there, waiting. But Apollo isn't finished yet. More astronauts are coming!
cap.2.7-b18.01: When my fender broke, the astronauts fixed it with duct tape and maps. Good as new!
cap.2.7-b18.02: Even on the Moon, sometimes the best tool is tape!
cap.2.7-b18.try: Astronauts fix things with what they have!
cap.2.7-b19.01: In December 1972, the last astronauts left the Moon. Nobody has walked here since. Not yet.
cap.2.7-b19.02: Not yet? Will people go back?
cap.2.7-b19.03: NASA is planning to! But first, let's see who is still watching the Moon.
cap.2.8-b20.01: I'm the Moon's photographer. From orbit I can still see the Apollo landers, rover tracks and even footpaths.
cap.2.8-b20.02: So it's true. They're all still there, right where they finished their work. LRO is still working today.
cap.2.8-b21.01: So many friends on the Moon! Now hold on. Our next trip is much, much longer. Next stop: Mars!
cap.3.1-b1.01: The Moon took three days. Mars takes about seven months! And we can't fly straight at it. Mars keeps moving, so we aim for where it will be.
cap.3.1-b1.02: Like throwing a ball to a friend who's running?
cap.3.1-b2.01: A radio message to Mars takes up to 22 minutes! So nobody can drive a Mars robot with a joystick. The robots have to be smart and careful on their own.
cap.3.1-b3.01: Mars is red because its dust has rust in it, like an old iron gate. It's colder than any freezer, and its air is so thin you couldn't breathe even for a second.
cap.3.2-b4.01: July 20th, 1976: exactly seven years after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, Viking 1 landed safely on Mars.
cap.3.2-b5.01: The first thing I photographed on Mars? My own foot. I wanted to check I'd landed on something solid!
cap.3.2-b5.02: Viking 1 sent the first pictures ever taken on the surface of Mars. It also tested the soil, looking for tiny signs of life.
cap.3.2-b5.04: No aliens! Scientists still talk about what its soil tests meant. That's okay. In science, 'we're not sure yet' is an honest answer.
cap.3.2-b6.01: Viking 1 kept working for more than six years. It went quiet in 1982 and is still sitting on that plain. Thank you, Viking!
cap.3.2b-b6b.01: After Viking, Mars waited 21 years. Then, on the 4th of July 1997, a new lander arrived. Boing! Boing! Boing! It landed in a ball of airbags!
cap.3.2b-b6c.01: I'm the first rover on Mars, as small as a microwave oven. I never went more than a few metres from my lander, but I was the first!
cap.3.2b-b6c.02: Sojourner was the first rover on another planet. Tiny, but it proved a rover can drive on another planet.
cap.3.3-b10.01: In 2018, a huge dust storm covered the whole planet. The Sun was hidden, and Opportunity's solar panels couldn't make power.
cap.3.3-b10.02: NASA called to it more than 1,000 times. It never answered. But it had done its job, and much, much more.
cap.3.3-b11.01: Goodbye, Oppy. Built for 90 days, you gave us almost 15 years. You are not forgotten.
cap.3.3-b7.01: Opportunity landed in a giant ball of airbags, bounced, and rolled straight into a little crater. A hole in one!
cap.3.3-b8.01: They told me I'd work for 90 days. I just... kept going. I drove more than a marathon: 45 kilometres!
cap.3.3-b8.02: Opportunity was planned for 90 days and explored for more than 14 years!
cap.3.3-b9.01: What's so special about this rock?
cap.3.3-b9.02: It has hematite, a mineral that forms in water. So long ago, Mars had water!
cap.3.3-b9.try: Hematite forms in water. Mars was once wet here!
cap.3.3b-b11b.01: Curiosity is as big as a car, too heavy for airbags. So NASA lowered it on ropes from a flying rocket crane. And look: every landing leaves parts behind, like breadcrumbs.
cap.3.3b-b11b.02: We protected the rovers through a fiery fall, then dropped away. Now we lie in the dust like a trail of breadcrumbs.
cap.3.3b-b11c.01: I'm climbing a mountain in an old lake bed, reading Mars's history layer by layer, like pages in a book.
cap.3.3b-b11c.02: Curiosity showed that Gale crater once held a lake where tiny living things, microbes, could have lived. And it's still working today!
cap.3.3c-b11d.01: I put my ear to the ground and heard Mars rumble more than a thousand times.
cap.3.3c-b11d.02: InSight recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and learned about Mars' core. Like a doctor listening to a heartbeat!
cap.3.3c-b11e.01: Bit by bit, dust covered its solar panels. In December 2022, InSight went quiet. Thank you for listening, InSight.
cap.3.4-b12.01: Landing on Mars takes about seven minutes, and the robot must do it all by itself. NASA engineers call it 'seven minutes of terror'!
cap.3.4-b13.01: Sure, I'm lying in the sand now. But I protected Perseverance on the way down. You're welcome!
cap.3.4-b13.02: These parts were used only once, for a few minutes. But without them, Perseverance couldn't have landed.
cap.3.4-b14.01: Psst... the parachute has a secret message hidden in its pattern. Engineers wrote it in computer code. Can you crack it?
cap.3.5-b15.01: This little helicopter is Ingenuity. It weighs about the same as two big bottles of water. Its job: try to fly on another planet. Nobody had ever done that.
cap.3.5-b15.02: But you said Mars has almost no air!
cap.3.5-b15.03: Right! So its blades spin super fast, about 2,400 times a minute. That's much faster than a helicopter on Earth.
cap.3.5-b16.01: I was supposed to fly 5 times. I flew 72 times!
cap.3.5-b16.02: The first powered flight on another planet! It was planned for five test flights. It flew 72!
cap.3.5-b17.01: In January 2024, on its 72nd flight, a blade broke, so it can't fly anymore. But every day it still wakes up, checks itself and saves data for future explorers who come to visit. A little hero, waiting on a sandy hill.
cap.3.5-b17.02: And Perseverance is still out there, exploring. Keep going, Percy!
cap.3.6-b18.01: I'm collecting pieces of Mars in little tubes, so that one day scientists on Earth can study them.
cap.3.6-b18.02: Perseverance is searching this old river delta for signs of past life. And it's still working today!
cap.3.6-b19.01: We are ten little tubes of Mars rock, left on the ground on purpose, waiting for a ride to Earth.
cap.3.6-b19.02: This is the first sample depot on another planet. These tubes aren't abandoned. They're waiting. Just like all our friends.
cap.3.6-b20.01: Mars, thank you! But some machines went even farther. Much, much farther. Ready?
cap.4.1-b1.01: Some machines never landed anywhere. They're still flying away from the Sun! Even my jetpack can't catch them.
cap.4.1-b2.01: 1972... I was the first to fly past Jupiter... I sent my last message in 2003. I'm still flying, quietly.
cap.4.1-b2.02: Pioneer 10 carries a metal plaque with a drawing that shows where it came from: Earth.
cap.4.1-b2b.01: I'm the only visitor Uranus and Neptune have ever had.
cap.4.1-b2b.02: Voyager 2 went into interstellar space in 2018. It's still sending data home today.
cap.4.1-b3.01: Launched in 1977. I'm the farthest thing people have ever made. I carry a golden record with sounds and music from Earth. And yes... I still call home.
cap.4.1-b3.02: On 18 November 2026, Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: its signal will take a whole day to reach us! It's in interstellar space, between the stars.
cap.4.1b-b3b.01: I showed the world Pluto's heart-shaped glacier.
cap.4.1b-b3b.02: After Pluto, New Horizons flew past Arrokoth in 2019, the farthest world ever explored up close. It's still working!
cap.4.2-b4.01: Look at all our friends! Some still work. Some went quiet. Some were used once, on purpose. But none of them are just junk. Each one taught us something.
cap.4.2-b5.01: See? Old doesn't mean abandoned. They're resting where they finished their work.
cap.4.3-b6.01: Perfect landing! See, I'm learning too.
cap.4.3-b7.01: Next time you look at the Moon, remember: there's a lander's bottom half up there, a car, footprints... and a little mirror that still answers when we call.
cap.4.3-b7b.01: And the story isn't over. In April 2026, four astronauts flew around the Moon, farther from Earth than any humans ever. NASA plans to land people near the Moon's south pole in 2028.
cap.4.3-b8.01: These machines were brave enough to go first. Maybe one day you'll build the next one. And when it finishes its work, someone like me will come and say thank you.
cap.deep-answer.01: The answer so far: out of the Sun's bubble, one light-day away, and still calling home.
cap.deep-question.01: Big question: how far can a machine we built travel?
cap.mars-answer.01: The answer so far: Mars once had water and places where life could have lived. The samples may tell us more.
cap.mars-question.01: Big question: could Mars once have been a home for tiny life?
cap.moon-answer.01: The answer so far: robots scouted first, people followed, and the mirrors and LRO still send us science.
cap.moon-question.01: Big question: how did we learn to land on the Moon, and what still works there today?
cap.tour-deep.01: And some never landed at all. They're still flying away from the Sun. Even my jetpack can't catch them!
cap.tour-map.01: Every glowing pin is a machine NASA sent out there. Watch them appear, year by year!
cap.tour-mars.01: Mars is much farther. Rovers, landers, parachutes and even a little helicopter live here.
cap.tour-moon.01: Up here on the Moon: cameras that crashed on purpose, landers, and three cars!
